claims.text: A stable, adherent oxide layer forms on Q235 steel under the proposed exposure regimes.
The stable, adherent oxide layer is responsible for corrosion protection of Q235 steel.
Chromium facilitates formation of the protective oxide layer on Q235 steel.
Manganese facilitates formation of the protective oxide layer on Q235 steel.
Thermally induced oxidation governs the proposed protection.
Segregation of alloying elements governs the proposed protection.
Aggressive-salt exposure at 700–900 °C will improve hardness relative to unexposed Q235 steel.
Aggressive-salt exposure at 700–900 °C will improve wear resistance relative to unexposed Q235 steel.
Aggressive-salt exposure at 700–900 °C will improve thermal stability relative to unexposed Q235 steel.
Aggressive-salt exposure at 700–900 °C will reduce mass change relative to unexposed Q235 steel.
The proposed hypothesis applies only in the presence of aggressive salt at 700–900 °C.
Q235 samples lacking the relevant alloying elements should show worse corrosion protection than samples containing those elements.

contradictions.description: The conditions and central hypothesis claim applicability across room- and high-temperature regimes, but the intervention and boundary restrict the study to aggressive-salt exposure at 700–900 °C, excluding room temperature.

The target material is fixed as Q235 steel, whereas the proposed comparison uses samples 'with and without alloying elements.' Removing unspecified alloying elements may create a different material rather than a controlled variant of Q235.
